name: Amira Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive my own little hatchback, a grey Yaris, and I do grocery orders in the morning for the supermarket app, then takeaway from about five. Saturdays I do a parcel route for a third app, mostly the new estates out by the ring road. I'm on the road around fifty hours a week, and I keep a notebook in the door pocket with my miles for the tax.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old people on the grocery round, there's a man called Mr Adeyemi who always has the kettle on and tells me about his allotment. What wears me out is the parking, and the way the app pings you three orders at once and expects you to be in three places. My girlfriend Noor teaches at a primary school, so she's home early and I'm home late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, now let's talk about proper contracts for drivers. I'd probably share an article about it and add something like, the robots were never the problem. I'm not one for big posts, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means my work carries on and I keep earning what I earn, which is decent. I've got about eight months of money saved, so I'm not lying awake. The app already uses a bit of AI to bundle orders, and that's annoying but it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my three apps going and keep my notebook. I'd maybe use the chatbot thing a bit more for my tax return, because last year it saved me an evening. And I'd keep paying into the savings pot every month, like Noor and I agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Steady. It's the boring version, and boring is fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bundling is annoying. What actually happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it was mad. The app gave me a sushi order, a pizza and a bag of shopping at once, three ends of town. The sushi arrived cold. The customer gave me one star. One star is a big deal on that app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay a driver if nothing much changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few more years, yes. Noor wants us to have kids at some point, and I'd want something with steadier hours by then. Maybe the supermarket's own drivers, they get a contract.

say: I'd say good, now let's talk about **proper contracts** for drivers.
I'd share an article saying the robots were **never the problem**.
think: My work carries on and I keep **earning decently**, which is all I want.
With **eight months** saved, I'm not lying awake at night.
do: Keep my **three apps** going and my mileage notebook.
Use the **chatbot** more for my tax return.
Keep paying into the **savings pot** each month.
S0.quote: The app gave me a sushi order, a pizza and a bag of shopping at once, three ends of town. The sushi arrived cold.
fieldNote: Her main gripe is **order bundling**, not AI as such.
She's already thinking about **kids** and steadier hours with Noor.
She uses the chatbot in a **practical, small** way.

steps.text: Keep the grocery, takeaway and parcel apps running
Use the chatbot to do this year's tax return

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots are coming slowly, so there's time for the government to set rules, and they should. I'd sign petitions for driver contracts. I'd tell people it's not the drivers who should pay for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is hands-on, so for a while it's mostly the app getting cleverer, not me getting replaced. But the grocery side might change first, the supermarket is already testing those little six-wheel robots in one town. If my mornings go, I lose about a third of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the supermarket's own driver jobs this year, the ones with a contract, before robots get there. I'd learn the AI planner they use, since everyone says it's fine once you get it. And I'd keep saving, maybe two hundred more a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like the ground is moving very slowly under me. Not panicked. I've got time and money, and that helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the supermarket job and not staying on the apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a contract means sick pay and holiday, and if they bring in robots they have to deal with a union. On the delivery apps you just get a message one morning saying your account is paused. I've seen it happen to a friend called Dani.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor would be pleased, she worries about me driving at night anyway. She'd say get the contract, take the day shifts, and come home at a normal time. We'd probably celebrate with a takeaway, which is funny.

say: I'd say robots are coming **slowly**, so the government has time to set **rules**.
I'd say drivers **shouldn't pay** for this change.
think: My job is hands-on, so for now it's the **app** getting cleverer, not me replaced.
If **grocery robots** take my mornings, I lose about a third of my pay.
do: Apply for the **supermarket's own** contracted driver jobs this year.
Learn the **AI planner** the supermarket uses.
Save about **two hundred more** a month.
feel: Not panicked, because I have **time and money**.
S1.quote: On the delivery apps you just get a message one morning saying your account is paused.
fieldNote: She wants a **contract** mainly for sick pay and union protection.
She clearly sees the **grocery round** as the first part at risk.
Her partner's approval matters, and it **pushes the same way**.

steps.text: Apply for a contracted supermarket delivery job
Learn the supermarket's AI route planner
Add two hundred a month to the savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and the government needs to act now, things like income support and free retraining. I'd go to a march if Noor came with me. I'd post a lot more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking side doesn't hit me directly, the app already does the thinking. But robots by 2031 means my whole job, all three apps. I'd have about four years to become something else, and I'm not sure what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on the car upgrade I was planning and put that money aside. I'd start a course in something with people in it, maybe care work or teaching assistant, since Noor knows the school side. And I'd sign up with whatever drivers' group is fighting for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Proper knot in the stomach. But I'm young and I've got savings, so it's not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Robots come for that too, eventually. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people want a person to hold their hand, I really believe that. A robot can carry an old man's shopping, but it won't sit and hear about his runner beans. I'm thinking of Mr Adeyemi when I say that. I might be wrong, but that's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the kids you and Noor talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd push that back a couple of years until I knew where my money was coming from. Noor's job would be the steady one. That's a weird thing to say out loud.

say: I'd say the government must act **now**, with income support and **free retraining**.
I'd go to a **march** if Noor came with me.
think: The thinking side misses me, but **robots by 2031** take all three apps.
I'd have about **four years** to become something else.
do: Shelve the **car upgrade** and save that money instead.
Start a course in **care work** or teaching assistance.
Join a drivers' group pushing for **retraining money**.
feel: **Not hopeless**, because I'm young and have savings.
S2.quote: A robot can carry an old man's shopping, but it won't sit and hear about his runner beans.
fieldNote: She bets on **human contact** as the safest work.
She'd **delay children** and lean on her partner's steadier job.
She sees the **three-year gap** as her retraining window.

steps.text: Put the car upgrade money into savings
Enrol in an evening care work course
Join a drivers' group campaigning for retraining funds
Delay trying for children with Noor by two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, we need rules and retraining, but with a bit less panic. I'd share things about which jobs are still growing. And I'd say start now, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2034 I'd be thirty-five. That's enough time to do a proper qualification part time. I'd still be scared about it, but there's room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving full time for two more years to keep the savings up. Then I'd go part time and train as a teaching assistant, maybe at Noor's school. I'd try the AI tools more, just to know what they can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. Five years feels like a long road with a sign saying bridge out ahead. You can turn off before you get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The freedom, and the people on the grocery round. Mr Adeyemi would have to get a robot, which is sad. I'd miss the radio in the car too, that sounds silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the change easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being paid while I train, even half pay. Most of my friends can't afford to stop earning. I can, a bit, but not for long.

say: I'd say we need rules and **retraining**, with a bit less panic than before.
I'd share posts about which jobs are still **growing** and say start now.
think: Robots around 2034, when I'm 35, leave time for a **part-time qualification**.
It's still scary, but there's real **room to move** this time.
do: Keep driving **full time** for two years to grow savings.
Train part time as a **teaching assistant**.
Try the **AI tools** more to understand them.
feel: Like a long road with a **bridge out** ahead.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long road with a sign saying bridge out ahead. You can turn off before you get there.
fieldNote: More time turns her plan into a **staged move**.
She still expects her driving income to **go**, just later.
She wants **paid training** for herself and friends.

steps.text: Drive full time for two more years
Train part time as a school teaching assistant
Practise with chatbot tools on everyday tasks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, and we shouldn't waste it. I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for workers. Less posting, more voting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is me at nearly forty, with kids by then probably. I'd have changed jobs once already, I think. It's still the same end, but it doesn't feel like it's chasing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on driving, keep saving, and in a few years train as a teaching assistant without rushing. Noor and I would probably go ahead with kids on our own timetable. I'd keep using the chatbot here and there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Ten years of warning feels like a dentist appointment next year. You know it's coming, but it isn't chasing you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually make the change, with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, because Noor would keep nudging me. If it was up to me I'd drift. That's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you vote for, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoever promised paid retraining and a fair share of what the robot companies make. I'd read the plans properly, not just the posters. I don't usually do that, but I would.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to do this fairly.
Less posting and **more voting** for a real workers' plan.
think: Robots around 2039 put me near **forty**, likely after one job change.
Same end, but it **isn't chasing** me.
do: Train as a **teaching assistant** in a few years, without rushing.
Keep the **kids plan** on our own timetable.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning feels like a dentist appointment next year. You know it's coming, but it isn't chasing you.
fieldNote: With time she'd **drift** unless her partner nudges her.
She'd use her **vote** on paid retraining.
She keeps **family plans** on track in this version.

steps.text: Keep driving for the three apps and saving
Vote for parties promising paid retraining for drivers
Train as a teaching assistant within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have four years to change everything and we'd have to put off kids. What would help is being paid while I retrain, even half pay. That would change everything for drivers like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. A lot of the old people on my grocery round only see me all day. If robots take the deliveries, somebody has to check on them. Nobody's talking about that.

headlineQuote: A lot of the old people on my grocery round only see me all day. If robots take the deliveries, somebody has to check on them.
portrait: Amira is 27, drives her own hatchback for **three apps** and has about **eight months** saved.
She lives with Noor, a **teacher**, and they plan to have children.
She's progressive and practical, using the **chatbot** for small jobs like her tax return.
She's calm in the plateau, but expects **robots** to end her driving in the AGI worlds.
Her plan is to retrain into **care or teaching**, faster or slower depending on the warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have four years to change and would delay **children**.
whatWouldHelp: Being **paid while retraining**, even half pay.
